subject: Archaeology
title: Linear A: Crete's Unbroken Code
description: A 60-second lesson on Linear A: Crete's Unbroken Code.

hook.text: The Minoans of Crete wrote in a script called Linear A. Over 1,400 inscriptions survive.

buildup.text: Linear B — a later script — was deciphered in 1952 and proved to be an early form of Greek.

discovery.text: Scholars can read the numbers and ideograms but not the language.

twist.text: The Minoan language is an isolate — unrelated to any known language.

climax.text: AI and computational linguistics are now tackling Linear A. Patterns are emerging, but no breakthrough has come yet.

punchline.text: We can count their sheep but not read their words.

quiz.question: Why is Linear A so difficult to decipher?
options: Only three inscriptions have been found so far
The Minoan language is unrelated to any known language, and no bilingual text exists
The script was intentionally designed as a secret code

details.summary: Linear A was the writing system of the Minoan civilization on Crete, used from roughly 1800 to 1450 BCE. Unlike Linear B, which was deciphered as an early form of Greek, Linear A records an unknown language and remains undeciphered despite many attempts.
details.whyItMatters: Deciphering Linear A would reveal the language and culture of the Minoans, Europe's first complex civilization. Without it, we know the Minoans through their material culture but cannot read their own words.
takeaways: Linear A was the writing system of the Minoan civilization
It records an unknown language unlike Linear B's Greek
Decipherment would unlock Europe's first complex civilization

faq.question: How does Linear A differ from Linear B?
faq.answer: Linear B, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, proved to be an early form of Greek used by Mycenaeans. Linear A uses similar-looking signs but records an entirely different, unknown language. Applying Linear B sound values to Linear A produces words in no known language.

faq.question: What types of texts survive in Linear A?
faq.answer: Most Linear A inscriptions are accounting records on clay tablets — inventories, offerings, and transactions. Some appear on religious objects, suggesting ritual use. The administrative nature of most texts limits what decipherment might reveal about Minoan literature or beliefs.
